title: Teen Archer Kumkum Mohod Wins Historic Asian Games Recurve Gold, Seals LA 2028 Olympic Quota
excerpt: The 17-year-old beat South Korea's Oh Yejin 10-8 in a shoot-off to become the first Indian woman to win the Asian Games individual recurve title, after securing India's LA 2028 quota place earlier in the day.
body:
• Seventeen-year-old Kumkum Anil Mohod defeated South Korea's Oh Yejin in a shoot-off — 10 to 8 — to win the women's individual recurve gold at the Asian Games on October 3, 2026, becoming the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games medal in the event.
  • Her semifinal victory over China's Jingyi Zhu, 6-2, secured one of two LA 2028 Olympic quota places for India. The quota belongs to the country, not the archer, so Mohod must still win selection trials closer to the Games to claim India's spot.
  • The teenager finished her Asian Games debut with three medals: team recurve gold with Ankita Bhakat and Kirti Sharma, mixed team silver with Dhiraj Bommadevara, and now the individual title.
  • In the quarterfinal she beat reigning world champion Kang Chaeyoung of South Korea 6-4 — defeating two Koreans, the sport's dominant nation, in a single day.

Opening news lead

Kumkum Mohod held her nerve when it mattered most. With the women's individual recurve final tied 5-5 on Saturday, the 17-year-old Indian archer shot a perfect 10 in the shoot-off while South Korea's Oh Yejin managed an 8, clinching the gold medal at the Asian Games and becoming the first Indian woman to medal in the event, according to The Hindu.

https://x.com/WeAreTeamIndia/status/2106227487441309914

The final was a slow-burn duel. Mohod opened the gold-medal match with sets of 27-29 and 29-29, took the third 30-29, then split the fourth and fifth 27-28 and 30-28 to force the one-arrow decider. One clean 10 later, India had a historic champion.

Context & Background

The morning had already been historic. In the semifinal, Mohod defeated China's Jingyi Zhu 6-2 (28-27, 30-30, 29-29, 29-28), a win that guaranteed India at least a silver — and, more consequentially, locked up one of the two quota places on offer for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Under the qualification rules, the quota goes to the nation, not the individual.

Her run through the draw was a tour of archery's elite. In the quarterfinal she dispatched reigning world champion Kang Chaeyoung 6-4, another South Korean. Defeating the world champion and an Olympic-caliber Korean in the same day, at 17, on her first Asian Games appearance, marks Mohod as one of the most consequential debutants India has produced in the sport.

Recurve archery at the Asian Games has been a Korean fortress for decades. India had never put a woman on the individual recurve podium before Saturday — not a bronze, let alone gold.

Impact & Analysis

"A historic first for Indian archery! This phenomenal triumph also secures a direct ticket to the LA 2028 Olympics."

— Mansukh Mandaviya, Union Sports Minister, on X

The Olympic quota is the result with the longest tail. India now has a guaranteed women's recurve slot for Los Angeles 2028, and a 17-year-old with the demonstrated ability to beat the best in the world under final-stage pressure is the strongest possible candidate to fill it — subject, as always, to the national selection process.

Mohod's medal haul at these Games reads like a full career condensed into days: gold in the women's team recurve alongside Ankita Bhakat and Kirti Sharma, silver in the mixed team with Dhiraj Bommadevara on Friday, and the individual crown on Saturday. The team gold was India's first in that event at the Asian Games; the mixed silver was the nation's first medal in that category too.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, Mohod's rise is the kind of story that travels far beyond the archery range — a teenager from India's domestic circuit standing up to Korean dominance on a one-arrow shot, carrying the first women's recurve gold home. Indian communities in Los Angeles will have particular reason to remember her name as 2028 approaches.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

The LA 2028 qualification cycle now opens in earnest for Indian archery. The country holds the quota; the next step is the national selection trials in the lead-up to the Games, where Mohod will need to re-earn the spot against domestic rivals. With the world champion already beaten at 17, the question is no longer whether India can compete with the Korean machine — it is whether Mohod can do it on Olympic soil.
